summary.title: The Single Most Important Internal Email in the History of Amazon
summary.one_liner: Internal communication structure (synchronous vs asynchronous, co-located vs distributed) shapes how organizations work, and Amazon's Bezos service-interface mandate shows how changing communication can enable a platform like AWS.
keywords: how to run a remote team
takeaways: Amazon's internal mandate that teams communicate only via externalizable service interfaces helped make AWS possible, illustrating Conway's Law.
Functional organizations (e.g., Apple) favor consistency but are slower; divisional organizations (e.g., Amazon's two-pizza teams) favor autonomy but are less consistent.
Asynchronous communication gives more optionality than synchronous, but requires more process, documentation and infrastructure up front.
Organizations can be synchronous or asynchronous regardless of physical location; co-located and distributed are separate dimensions.
summary.summary: The author, building on an earlier essay on remote work, argues that an organization's internal communication system is a major lever on productivity. Using Steve Yegge's 'Google Platforms Rant' and Bezos's internal service-interface email as examples, the piece contrasts functional and divisional organization structures and cites Netflix's 'highly aligned, loosely coupled' principle as a hybrid. It then maps communication frameworks on a synchronous-to-asynchronous spectrum, combined with co-located versus distributed setups, using Apple, Amazon, InVision and Basecamp as examples. It closes with the claim that asynchronous communication offers the most optionality but has high upfront maintenance costs.
